title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] Fatphobia is a form of discrimination that negatively impacts physical and mental health. Adolescents in health-related technical education are both exposed to and capable of reproducing fatphobia. This study aimed to analyze the perceptions of adolescent students in professional technical health courses regarding fatphobia and its relationship with social media.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] This qualitative study was conducted with 24 adolescents aged 14 to 18 years enrolled in Nursing and Aesthetics technical programs at a public technical school in Fortaleza, Brazil. Two focus group sessions were held, one for each program, using a semi-structured guide. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Descending Hierarchical Classification with the IRaMuTeQ software. The analysis sought to identify thematic patterns based on the frequency and association of textual segments. The study followed established qualitative reporting criteria to ensure transparency and rigor.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] Five thematic classes emerged: (1) Recognition and reproduction of fatphobia; (2) Experience of fatphobia; (3) Social construction of the “ideal body”; (4) The fat body and the reinterpretation of health; and (5) Influence of social media and use of digital filters. Students recognized the existence and harmful effects of fatphobia but also acknowledged reproducing stigmatizing comments and behaviors. Students demonstrated nuanced views about the relationship between body size and health, challenging weight-centered biomedical interpretations. Social media emerged as a powerful driver of unrealistic aesthetic expectations.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [abstract] Adolescents in technical health training recognize fatphobia as both an individual and structural issue, shaped by social norms and amplified by social media. Although they express empathy toward people with larger bodies, many simultaneously reproduce weight-stigmatizing practices. Technical-vocational schools represent formative spaces where fatphobia is simultaneously reproduced and questioned, making them key environments for integrating educational interventions that promote body diversity, challenge weight-based prejudice, and support the development of more inclusive future health professionals.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] Fatphobia, understood as prejudice and bias directed at people with bodies categorized as fat, impacts individuals’ physical, psychological, and social health [1]. It is a form of discrimination that affects adults, children, and adolescents alike [2], and is reproduced through scientific discourse and institutional practices, manifesting in various contexts, such as educational settings [3], social media [4], and healthcare services [5]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] . In this study, we adopt the following conceptual distinctions: “fatphobia” refers to the sociocultural and political structures that devalue fat bodies and uphold thinness as a normative ideal [1]; and “obesity” and “overweight” are used strictly as biomedical categories [2], mentioned when referring to dominant clinical discourses or institutional classifications.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] In the healthcare field, fatphobia influences interactions between healthcare professionals and patients with fat bodies, resulting in delayed diagnoses, reduced quality of care, and adverse health outcomes [6]. The use of stigmatizing language and the belief that weight is entirely controllable through individual effort compromise the therapeutic bond and hinder treatment adherence, even among children and adolescents [7]. As a result, overweight individuals often delay or avoid seeking medical care, even when faced with serious and treatable conditions, due to fear of judgment or previous negative experiences [8].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] The literature indicates that professionals recognize limitations in their competencies to address larger bodies, reporting insecurity and inadequate educational training [9]. Education about fatphobia and obesity is limited in both content and depth in the curricula of health professional training programs. These programs still do not adequately address the multifactorial determinants of body weight, the psychosocial implications of fatphobia, or practical strategies to reduce it [3, 10].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] Fatphobia among undergraduate health students is present even at the beginning of their studies, with negative weight stereotypes attributed primarily to personal flaws or lack of willpower [11–13]. A study comparing health students at different stages of their studies found that students with lower educational levels (high school) were more likely to show fatphobia than those pursuing or completing a master’s degree [10]. However, a systematic literature review indicates that the influence of education on fatphobia remains inconclusive, as studies have shown conflicting results [14].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] On social media, adolescents are more exposed to fatphobia, with this exposure influenced by both the time spent using the platform and the type of content consumed by this audience [15]. Furthermore, the idealization of thin bodies on social media intensifies body dissatisfaction, negatively impacting adolescents’ physical and mental health [16].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Introduction] Adolescents in professional training in the health field are a target group for further study, as they are most affected by social media exposure and will also be future care agents capable of reproducing or modifying fatphobic practices. Therefore, this study aimed to analyze the perceptions of adolescent students in professional technical courses in the health field regarding fatphobia and its relationship with social media. Our interpretation is guided by the understanding that such perceptions are not merely descriptive but are embedded in broader processes of subjectivation, symbolic violence, and professional socialization within health training contexts.

section: Influence of social media and use of digital filters
text: [Influence of social media and use of digital filters] The organization of the categories presented does not imply that they are independent; rather, it serves as a descriptive strategy to highlight the interconnections and overlaps among them. For instance, the recognition of fatphobia (Class 1) coexists with its reproduction through digital culture (Class 5), while resistance to dominant health and beauty narratives (Classes 3 and 4) emerges in tension with normalized stigma expressed in daily interactions (Class 2).

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Adolescents recognize the negative impacts of fatphobia and acknowledge it as a structural phenomenon, reinforced by social media, while also admitting to reproducing fatphobic discourses. This duality of perceptions highlights the internalization of aesthetic standards and the development of critical consciousness, possibly influenced by adolescence itself and the educational context in health programs. These perceptions are not isolated opinions but are shaped by the socialization processes of technical health education, which both challenge and reinforce fatphobic discourse

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . Unlike prior studies focused on university-level students, our findings show that these dynamics begin earlier: students in technical programs, though not yet exposed to full clinical practice, already negotiate professional values influenced by biomedical models and aesthetic ideals.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Students identified that fatphobic behaviors are often naturalized and interpreted as “jokes” or harmless comments. This situation is similar to Pierre Bourdieu’s [22] concept of symbolic violence, which describes subtle forms of domination based on the unconscious acceptance of values and hierarchies imposed by the dominant culture. In the context of fatphobia, this violence is related to practices such as attributing negative characteristics to people with fat bodies (e.g., lack of self-control or incompetence), which become socially acceptable and even legitimized [23].

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Reports of personal or witnessed experiences of discrimination in public and family spaces reinforce that fatphobia acts as a form of everyday violence. Family members, especially parents and siblings, can be common sources of fatphobia, often manifested through criticism, judgment, jokes, and weight-related teasing [24]. In public spaces, the lack of physical adaptations causes embarrassment and limits participation in common activities, such as accessing health services, leisure, and transportation. Therefore, people with larger bodies often avoid public environments or situations where they may be exposed to judgment or physical inadequacy [8, 25, 26]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . Interpreting these experiences through the lens of symbolic violence highlights how fatphobia operates not only through overt discrimination, but also through normalized practices that remain unquestioned within everyday social and educational contexts.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] The coexistence of empathy and complicity in students’ statements suggests that technical training environments both expose and reproduce fatphobia. While students begin to reflect critically on fatphobic experiences, their narratives also reveal a lack of institutional framing to support that reflection. This highlight missed opportunities within technical curricula to foster more inclusive understandings of body size and health [17]. These patterns are also shaped by adolescence, a developmental period when body identity is still being constructed and is influenced by social norms and peer belonging [27]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . This suggests that, without intentional pedagogical intervention, technical education risks reinforcing social norms that pathologize fat bodies at the moment when students are beginning to form their professional and moral identities.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] While some students demonstrate empathy and question weight-based norms, they also reproduce stigmatizing attitudes, revealing an ambivalent stance shaped by early professional socialization. This contradiction suggests that the process of becoming a health professional is tied to subjectivation, whereby students internalize institutional norms that both challenge and sustain fatphobic discourse. Although critical awareness begins to emerge, it remains fragile due to the lack of pedagogical support. These patterns align with prior research showing that health education often overlooks the psychosocial dimensions of fatphobia and the complex determinants of body weight [10]

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . Additionally, the hidden curriculum, comprising implicit norms and values, can reinforce dominant ideologies within training environments [28, 29]. Without pedagogical efforts to deconstruct fatphobic norms, technical health training may inadvertently serve as a site for the reproduction of fatphobia.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] As an early entry point into the health field, technical training introduces not only practical competencies but also implicit notions of body image within healthcare. This context intensifies key tensions (empathy versus stigma reproduction, and critical discourse versus everyday practice) by immersing students in dominant health discourses before they develop the critical awareness necessary to question them. Therefore, curricular design at the technical level should not be limited to clinical content but must actively engage with social and structural determinants of health, including fatphobia.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] The ideal of a thin and curvy body is evident in adolescents’ statements. This standard, known as slim-thick, is considered more harmful to mental health than the traditional thin ideal, as it requires the simultaneous pursuit of thinness and curves, a goal difficult to achieve without invasive interventions or unhealthy practices [30]. The search for this type of body is influenced by advertising, social media, and digital influencers, leading teenagers, especially females, to seek not only thinness but also curves in specific areas of the body [31]. The prominence of the slim-thick ideal in students’ narratives underscores how aesthetic norms penetrate health training spaces, conflicting with inclusive and health-centered professional values.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] By pointing out that weight should not be the sole indicator of health, adolescents demonstrate an affinity with approaches such as Health At Every Size (HAES), which proposes a non-pathologizing understanding of fat bodies and emphasizes person-centered care rather than weight [30]. Body weight alone is not a reliable marker of health. Weight-based measures, such as the Body Mass Index (BMI), are independent of key metabolic markers (e.g., blood pressure, lipid profile, and glycated hemoglobin); thus, people with the same weight may present different metabolic health profiles [32]. Strategies that prioritize healthy behaviors and well-being are considered more effective for promoting comprehensive health [33]

This challenges the reductionist logic of the biomedical model and opens space for understandings of health that resist the pathologization of fat bodies.

text: [Discussion] Adolescents report routinely using digital filters on social media to enhance desired physical characteristics, indicating a link between the beauty standards promoted on these platforms and dissatisfaction with self-image. The practice of manipulating photos with filters influences adolescents to negatively compare their bodies to edited versions of themselves or others [34]. Digital influencers intensify this process by promoting the “ideal body” as a consumer product, supposedly attainable through weight-loss products and restrictive eating habits, and by associating it with health, beauty, and happiness [35]

This highlights the need to critically address digital cultures within health education, as unexamined exposure to idealized imagery may reinforce fatphobic attitudes about bodies and health.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] It is possible to observe the attempt to resignify their own image, as indicated by statements that recognize their own beauty and the natural diversity of bodies. Body-positive content (a movement that promotes self-compassion and body acceptance) is growing on social media and is associated with increased positive self-image thinking [37–39]. A study with adolescents and young adults revealed that these groups recognize the relevance of body-positive posts for self-acceptance, although some still demonstrate resistance to this content due to internalized beauty ideals [40]. This coexistence of discourses highlights the complexity of social media interactions and their role in shaping divergent perceptions regarding the body.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Our study contributes to the literature by showing how technical-vocational schools may act as formative spaces where normative discourses around bodies are established and reinforced. This has important implications for early professional identity formation, particularly in health-related fields where body ideals are often implicitly associated with notions of competence and self-discipline. Without targeted pedagogical interventions, these biases may be internalized and carried into future healthcare practice.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Like all qualitative research, this study does not aim to generalize its findings but rather to offer an in-depth understanding of adolescent perceptions within a specific institutional and cultural context. Some limitations should be acknowledged. The focus group format may have introduced social desirability bias, as participants might have moderated their responses due to the presence of peers or researchers, particularly when addressing sensitive topics such as body image and fatphobia. The predominantly female composition of the sample may have influenced the themes that emerged, especially those related to beauty standards and social media use

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] . The institutional affiliation of the researchers with health education programs may have shaped the discussions, reinforcing professional or normative perspectives. These contextual factors should be considered when interpreting the findings, as they may have influenced both the content and tone of participants’ responses. Additionally, the research was conducted in only one public technical school in Fortaleza, in Northeast Brazil, where specific cultural values and aesthetic norms may prevail, which may limit the transferability of results to other regions or educational settings; therefore, the findings may not be transferable to settings with different sociocultural perceptions of body image and fatphobia.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Discussion] Despite these limitations, the use of focus groups and analysis with the IRaMuTeQ software enabled greater depth in interpreting the statements, revealing symbolic aspects of fatphobia that would be difficult to capture through quantitative approaches. This study offers analytically insights into an understudied educational context, highlighting processes that are likely present, though variably expressed, in other technical health training settings.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Conclusion] Adolescents undergoing technical training in healthcare recognize the existence and impacts of fatphobia, both individually and structurally. While demonstrating critical awareness of the discrimination faced by fat people, participants also recognize their own participation in the reproduction of fatphobic practices. The influence of social media, particularly through the use of filters and the propagation of difficult-to-achieve aesthetic standards, was recognized as an important factor in the construction of self-image and the perception of the ideal body, reinforcing discriminatory behaviors.

title: Fatphobia among adolescents: how future health professionals perceive weight-related violence and the influence of social media
text: [Conclusion] The adolescents’ statements highlight the need for educational approaches that promote respect for body diversity and the deconstruction of fatphobia. Vocational schools, as spaces for professional and critical training, can be a strategic environment for developing more inclusive and anti-discriminatory care practices. It is essential that these institutions incorporate content and pedagogical practices that enable future professionals to recognize and avoid fatphobic practices within healthcare settings.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] The differentiation of macrophages into foam cells is a hallmark of atherosclerotic plaques, and macrophage polarization is a key driver of disease progression, yet the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. We employed summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) combined with transcriptomic validation to explore causal relationships and validate findings at the tissue level.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] We integrated multi-omics data, including DNA methylation (mQTLs), gene expression (eQTLs), and protein expression (pQTLs), from GeneCards and GWAS summary statistics from FinnGen and UK Biobank. SMR and colocalization analyses were used to identify causal associations. Tissue-specific validation was conducted using eQTL data from artery tissues, and transcriptome analysis was performed using GEO datasets to confirm gene expression patterns in atherosclerotic tissues, followed by confirmation in clinical samples. The function of key genes were explored using Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] SMR and colocalization analyses identified 41 methylation sites, 2 genes (DNMT3A and DLGAP5), and 1 protein associated with atherosclerosis. Specifically, methylation site cg10130446 in DLGAP5 was negatively correlated with atherosclerosis, while sites cg08485187 and cg17742416 in DNMT3A were positively associated. Tissue-specific validation revealed that SIRT6 gene expression was linked to atherosclerosis risk in aortic and tibial artery tissues. Transcriptome analysis from GEO database and blood samples confirmed elevated DLGAP5 and SIRT6 expressions.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [abstract] This study integrates SMR with transcriptomic validation to reveal causal links between macrophage polarization-related genes and atherosclerosis. Key genes DNMT3A, DLGAP5, and SIRT6 were identified as significant candidate regulatory factors. Tissue-specific validation and GEO-based transcriptome analysis provided robust evidence supporting these findings, highlighting the importance of macrophage polarization in atherosclerosis pathogenesis and offering new insights for therapeutic intervention.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Atherosclerosis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by lipid accumulation in large arteries [1]. As the leading cause of cardiovascular diseases, it accounts for approximately one-third of global deaths, with increasing prevalence worldwide [2–4]. Despite established risk factors such as hyperlipidemia and hypertension [5], the persistent burden of AS underscores the urgent need to elucidate its underlying mechanisms.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Macrophages are crucial immune cells involved in the inflammatory response associated with atherosclerosis [6]. Upon entering the arterial intima, monocytes differentiate into macrophages and can adopt different functional phenotypes based on the local microenvironment. These phenotypes are broadly categorized into M1 and anti-inflammatory (M2) macrophages [6–8]. The balance between M1 and M2 macrophages plays a pivotal role in the progression or regression of atherosclerotic lesions. Advanced single-cell sequencing technologies have revealed the heterogeneity of macrophage populations within atherosclerotic plaques, highlighting the complexity of macrophage polarization and its impact on disease pathology [9]

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Genes involved in macrophage polarization, encompassing those encoding cytokines, transcription factors, and receptors, have been implicated in the modulation of atherosclerotic processes [11]. Notably, key transcriptional regulators such as NF-κB, STAT1, and PPAR-γ play pivotal roles in orchestrating the M1/M2 balance [12]. Previous investigations, ranging from Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) to Mendelian Randomization (MR) analyses, have consistently detected associations between these inflammatory mediators and atherosclerosis [13, 14]. However, a critical limitation in current literature is the conflation of general inflammatory signaling with the specific genetic drivers of macrophage polarization

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] . For instance, while loci such as NFKB1 or PPARG are robustly linked to atherosclerosis, their extensive involvement in broad systemic immune responses makes it difficult to pinpoint whether their pathogenicity stems specifically from the modulation of macrophage polarization mechanisms or merely from generalized systemic inflammation [15, 16]. Consequently, the precise causal architecture—specifically, whether genetic variations within the polarization machinery directly drive atherogenesis independent of systemic inflammatory burdens—remains incompletely elucidated.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Mendelian randomization (MR) is an innovative analytical approach that leverages genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between exposures and outcomes. Unlike observational studies, MR is robust to reverse causation and minimizes confounding, thereby significantly enhancing the accuracy and reliability of its findings [17]. Building on this foundation, summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) has emerged as a powerful extension of MR. SMR enables researchers to explore genetic associations between various molecular traits—such as gene expression, DNA methylation, or protein levels—and diseases of interest using large-scale genomic datasets [18]

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] . By utilizing top cis-quantitative trait loci (cis-QTLs) as exposure variables, SMR achieves greater statistical power, especially when analyses are conducted with independent samples of substantial size. Prior research has demonstrated the efficacy of SMR in identifying and validating pathogenic genes linked to atherosclerosis [19]. Therefore, this approach provides a comprehensive perspective of causal inference between targeted genes and the disease.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Background] Given the crucial role of macrophage polarization in atherosclerosis, this study aimed to identify potential macrophage polarization-related genes in the disease using SMR methods. Using comprehensive multi-omics analysis, this study aims to reveal the complex genetic factors behind atherosclerosis and macrophage polarization. We expect that these findings will not only increase the understanding of the mechanism of the disease, but also provide important theoretical guidance for the development of precision treatment programs and personalized medical pathways.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Study design] The present investigation employed a comprehensive, stepwise approach to elucidate the role of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis susceptibility. As depicted in Fig. 1, our study began by identifying a total of 731 protein-coding genes related to macrophage polarization through the GeneCards database. To strengthen the credibility of our findings, we incorporated instrumental variables selection, utilizing data from three large-scale studies for mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL instruments. Subsequently, we leveraged GWAS data from two independent cohorts - the discovery set from the FinnGen database, and the replication set from the UK Biobank (UKB), followed by SMR and colocalization analysis to confirm the causal relationships between the identified genes and atherosclerosis

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Study design] . After identifying the candidate genes with causal associations, we further performed tissue-specific validation to explore the causal relationship between identified gene expression in tissues and atherosclerosis. Finally, transcriptome analysis was performed using data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database to validate the expression of candidate genes in atherosclerotic tissues. The function of these genes were investigated with enrichment analysis and gene-gene network was generated to illustrate their functional associations. Finally, the expression of the key genes identified in this study were confirmed in clinical samples

text: [Study design] . Finally, the expression of the key genes identified in this study were confirmed in clinical samples. These methods enabled us to integrate evidence from various omics levels, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the macrophage polarization-related genes and their impact on atherosclerosis susceptibility. title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Summary-data-based MR analysis] In this study, we extended our investigation into the causal relationships between quantitative trait loci (QTLs)—specifically, methylation QTLs (mQTL), expression QTLs (eQTL), and protein QTLs (pQTL)—and atherosclerosis. We also explored the potential causal associations between mQTL and eQTL by framing mQTL as the exposure variable and eQTL as the outcome variable. To enhance the analysis, we developed an advanced multi-SNP-based summary data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) method (--smr-multi), which incorporates multiple single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within QTL regions [27]

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Summary-data-based MR analysis] . This method integrates all SNPs in a window centered on the QTL ± 500 kb in SMR analysis, whose p value is less than the default value 5.0 × 10− 8, and the LD r2 value of top-related SNPs is less than the default value 0.9. To distinguish between pleiotropic effects and linkage, we applied the heterogeneity in dependent instruments (HEIDI) test. A P-HEIDI value greater than 0.05 indicates that the observed associations are unlikely due to pleiotropy. By setting thresholds of P_SMR_multi < 0.05, P_SMR < 0.05, and P-HEIDI > 0.05, we identified results that met these criteria for further colocalization analyses among mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL, as well as for integration analysis.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Summary-data-based MR analysis] Our analytic framework was rigorously designed to satisfy the three core assumptions of Mendelian randomization: relevance, independence, and exclusion restriction. The relevance assumption was ensured by selecting top cis-QTLs with genome-wide significance (P < 5.0 × 10− 8) as instrumental variables, guaranteeing a strong association with the exposure. To address the independence and exclusion restriction assumptions, we applied the HEIDI test to distinguish true causality from linkage disequilibrium (LD) or horizontal pleiotropy. A P-HEIDI > 0.05 was strictly used as the criterion to filter out pleiotropic signals, thereby supporting the inference that the genetic instruments affect atherosclerosis risk solely through the target molecular traits.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Colocalization analysis] Colocalization analysis was conducted using the ‘coloc’ R package to identify shared causal variants between AR and macrophage polarization-related mQTLs, eQTLs and pQTLs. Five mutually exclusive hypotheses were tested: (1) H0: No association with SNPs in the region for either trait; (2) H1: Association with SNPs in the region for trait 1 only; (3) H2: Association with SNPs in the region for trait 2 only; (4) H3: Association with SNPs in the region for both traits, but with different causal variants; (5) H4: Association with SNPs in the region for both traits, sharing the same causal variant

section: Multi-omics integration and gene prioritization strategy
text: [Multi-omics integration and gene prioritization strategy] To systematically identify key genes, we employed a hierarchical prioritization strategy. First, genes were screened for significant causal associations (P_SMR < 0.05) in at least one omics level (mQTL, eQTL, or pQTL), with pleiotropy excluded by the HEIDI test (P_HEIDI > 0.05). Second, we prioritized candidates showing consistent evidence across multiple omics layers, specifically focusing on the intersection of mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL hits. Finally, these candidates were rigorously validated using tissue-specific eQTL data and clinical differential expression analysis to confirm their biological relevance.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Discussion] This study investigated the causal relationships between macrophage polarization-related genetic factors and atherosclerosis using SMR approach. We integrated genetic data from mQTL, eQTL, and pQTL analyses to identify key genes associated with atherosclerosis. Upon integrating the multi-omics data, we identified two genes associated with atherosclerosis risk: DNMT3A and DLGAP5. Additionally, the expression of the SIRT6 gene demonstrated a significant association with atherosclerosis risk in both aortic and tibial artery tissues. Transcriptomic analysis using further confirmed the elevated expression of DLGAP5 and SIRT6 in atherosclerosis patients, supporting their role in disease progression.

text: [Discussion] Among the key genes identified, DLGAP5 and DNMT3A stood out with robust evidence linking them to atherosclerosis. DLGAP5 is known to function as an oncoprotein, playing significant roles in multiple cancer types by promoting cell proliferation, migration, and invasion [29]. Specifically, in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), DLGAP5 exhibits high expression levels compared to normal liver tissues, and its elevated expression correlates with poor clinical outcomes and tumor immune cell infiltration, indicating its potential role in modulating the tumor microenvironment [30]. Furthermore, studies have shown that DLGAP5 promotes gallbladder cancer (GBC) progression and induces macrophage M2 polarization through the activation of the cAMP pathway, enhancing tumor growth and metastasis [31]

Although direct evidence linking DLGAP5 to macrophage polarization in ovarian cancer is limited, the gene’s impact on cancer development and immune response suggests a possible indirect effect on the tumor-associated macrophages. Collectively, although direct evidence linking DLGAP5 with atherosclerosis is lacking, current findings suggests that DLGAP5 may modulate macrophage polarization and therefore results in various disease

text: [Discussion] . Our study indicated that DLGAP5’s methylation site cg10130446 demonstrated a significant negative association with atherosclerosis risk, suggesting that higher methylation levels at this site reduce DLGAP5 expression, which in turn lowers disease risk. Furthermore, the elevated expression of DLGAP5 was confirmed in atherosclerotic tissues and blood samples. Further research is needed to elucidate the relationship between DLGAP5 and atherosclerosis and clarify the mechanism by which DLGAP5 affects this condition.

title: Integrative multi-omics analysis of macrophage polarization-related genes in atherosclerosis development
text: [Discussion] DNMT3A, a methyltransferase critical for de novo DNA methylation, has emerged as a key regulator in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis through its epigenetic modifications that influence gene expression and cellular function. Mutations in DNMT3A associated with clonal hematopoiesis promote a pro-inflammatory state in macrophages, leading to increased activation of inflammatory pathways and accelerated atherosclerotic lesion development, a mechanism comparable to that observed with TET2 mutations [33]. DNMT3A also impacts m6A RNA methylation, a key post-transcriptional regulatory mechanism, which may influence endothelial cell adhesion and smooth muscle cell proliferation, contributing to plaque formation and instability [34]

text: [Discussion] . Additionally, loss-of-function mutations in DNMT3A are linked to altered DNA methylation patterns in macrophages, which promote inflammasome activation and cytokine secretion, amplifying chronic inflammation in atherosclerotic plaques [35]. Furthermore, DNMT3A deficiency leads to several potentially pro-atherogenic phenotypes in various immune cell populations, including pro-inflammatory activation of mast cells [36], increased IFNγ production by T cells, and reduced immunosuppressive function in myeloid-derived suppressor cells. Conversely, DNMT3A inhibition has been shown to increase IL-13 expression in T cells and limit type I interferon production in macrophages, which could protect against atherosclerosis development [37, 38]

The negative regulatory relationship between methylation at cg08485187 and cg17742416 and DNMT3A expression suggests that epigenetic dysregulation may contribute to increased disease risk, underscoring the need for targeted investigations into macrophage polarization-mediated pathways.

SIRT6, a member of the sirtuin family of NAD-dependent deacetylases, has been shown to play a crucial role in various cardiovascular pathologies [39, 40]. SIRT6 is unique due to its chromatin-associated deacetylase activity, which imparts several protective effects similar to those of SIRT1 [41–43]. These include inhibition of heart failure and slowing down the aging process in mice [44, 45]

text: [Ex Vivo Fluorescence Imaging of NS Distribution] To circumvent signal attenuation caused by dorsal hair scattering, ex vivo imaging was performed to monitor the biodistribution of NS-PTEN. Animals were sacrificed at designated time points via inhalation of CO2 in strict accordance with IACUC protocols. Spinal cord tissues were immediately harvested and positioned on the imaging stage of a Davinch-Invivo Imaging System (INV-16M, Davinch, Korea). This system is equipped with a high-sensitivity cooled CCD camera (−50 °C) and a motorized 12-position filter wheel. Fluorescence images were acquired under standardized exposure conditions, and signals were quantified as total radiant efficiency (p/s/cm2/sr)/(μW/cm2) using the manufacturer’s analysis software, with all values normalized to background tissue fluorescence.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [abstract] Substantial oxidative stress during myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury precipitates cell death and heart failure, for which translatable redox therapies remain scarce. Here, we show that nicotinamide riboside kinase 2 (NMRK2) is rapidly upregulated after reperfusion and exerts redox protection by a previously unrecognized mechanism. We established myocardial I/R injury in mice and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) injury in cardiomyocytes. By elevating NADPH, restoring NAD+/NADH, increasing GSH/GSSG and activating Trx1, NMRK2 overexpression enhanced cellular antioxidant capacity and reduced oxidative damage during both myocardial I/R and cellular H/R injury. Knockdown of NAD kinase (NADK) abolished these protective effects

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [abstract] . Knockdown of NAD kinase (NADK) abolished these protective effects. Mechanistically, nucleocytoplasmic fractionation and immunofluorescence confirmed robust Yes-associated protein (YAP) nuclear entry in NMRK2-overexpressing cells; Co-IP revealed NMRK2-induced disruption of the integrin β–YAP interaction; knockdown of integrin β reduced NADK expression and increased YAP phosphorylation at Ser127; and ChIP-qPCR and luciferase assays demonstrated that YAP directly binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) for its transcriptional activation. In conclusion, NMRK2 sustains redox protection by disrupting the integrin β–YAP complex and driving YAP-dependent NADK transcription, providing a readily translatable therapy against myocardial I/R injury.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Introduction] Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains the foremost complication of reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction [[1], [2], [3]]. While restoration of coronary blood flow limits infarct size, it simultaneously triggers an oxidative burst that depletes NADPH, overwhelms the glutathione (GSH) and thioredoxin (Trx) antioxidant systems, and precipitates cardiomyocyte death [[4], [5], [6], [7]]. Effective redox-targeted interventions applicable to this acute reperfusion window remain an urgent unmet clinical need.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Introduction] NADPH regeneration depends on NAD kinase (NADK)-mediated phosphorylation of NAD+ to NADP+ [8]; making NADK an attractive target for restoring redox balance during early reperfusion. Nicotinamide riboside kinase 2 (NMRK2), the rate-limiting enzyme of the NAD+ salvage pathway, is markedly upregulated within 24 h of reperfusion [9,10]. However, whether it governs NADK transcription or merely supports NAD+ synthesis is unknown. Consequently, the signaling cascades that acutely upregulate NADK during myocardial I/R injury remain undefined.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Introduction] Here, we demonstrate that NMRK2 mobilizes the Yes-associated protein (YAP)–NADK pathway to replenish NADPH during early reperfusion, thereby restoring the GSH and Trx antioxidant systems and attenuating injury following myocardial I/R in mice and hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) in cardiomyocytes. We present a previously unrecognized NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis positions NADK as a signal-responsive redox node and offer a translatable strategy for acute cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury.

text: [Live/dead cell staining] Cell death was assessed using the LIVE/DEAD Cell Imaging Kit (Thermo Fisher R37601). Live cells were labeled with calcein-AM, which is enzymatically converted into green-fluorescent calcein, whereas dead cells were identified by red fluorescence from ethidium homodimer-1 staining of cells with compromised membranes. Following H/R, AC16 and H9c2 cells were incubated with a 2 × working solution at 22 °C for 15 min. Fluorescent signals were immediately captured using a fluorescence microscope, with live cells appearing green and dead cells appearing red. text: [Flow cytometry] Apoptosis was quantified using Annexin V-FITC/PI double staining (Beyotime C1062 M). text: [Nuclear and cytoplasmic protein extraction] Nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins were isolated from cardiomyocytes using the Cytoplasmic and Nuclear Protein Extraction Kit (Beyotime P0027). section: RNA extraction and Real-time quantitative PCR
text: [RNA extraction and Real-time quantitative PCR] Total RNA was extracted from heart tissue using Trizol reagent (Thermo Fisher 15596026). RNA quality and purity were evaluated using UV spectrophotometry (NanoDrop 2000; Thermo Fisher) by measuring absorbance at 260 and 280 nm, respectively. For cDNA synthesis, 1 μg total RNA was used as the template. The qPCR reaction mixture contained 5 μL SYBR qPCR SuperMix (Novoprotein E096-01A), 1 μL forward and reverse primers, 1 μL cDNA, and 2 μL RNase-free water. Cycling conditions included 40 amplifications followed by melting curve analysis. Target gene (NMRK2, NADK) expression was normalized to β-tubulin using the 2−ΔΔCt method; primers were synthesized by Qingke Biotechnology (Beijing).

Cardiomyocytes were lysed in ice-cold IP lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. After centrifugation at 12,000×g for 15 min at 4 °C, equal amounts of total protein were incubated overnight at 4 °C with anti-integrin β1 antibody or control IgG, followed by incubation with protein A/G agarose beads for 2 h. The beads were then washed extensively with lysis buffer, and bound proteins were eluted by boiling in SDS sample buffer. text: [Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR] ChIP assays were performed using a commercial ChIP kit (CST 9005S) to assess the binding of YAP to the NADK promoter. Cardiomyocytes were cross-linked with 1% formaldehyde at room temperature for 10 min and quenched with glycine. Cells were then lysed, and chromatin was sheared by sonication to obtain DNA fragments of approximately 200–500 bp. The fragmented chromatin was incubated overnight at 4 °C with an anti-YAP antibody or normal IgG as a negative control. Immunocomplexes were captured using protein A/G magnetic beads, washed extensively, and eluted. Cross-links were reversed, and DNA was purified and analyzed by qPCR using primers targeting the NADK promoter. Results were normalized to input DNA and presented as fold enrichment over IgG controls.

Cardiomyocytes were co-transfected with these constructs and a YAP expression plasmid or control vector, along with a Renilla luciferase plasmid as an internal control. Luciferase activity was measured 24–48 h later using a dual-luciferase assay system. Firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity and expressed as relative luciferase activity.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] Earlier studies have established NMRK2 as a key enzyme in NAD+ salvage pathway and documented its metabolic importance in in heart and skeletal muscle [9,18]. NMRK2 is markedly upregulated in ischemic and hypertensive conditions, and confers protection by suppressing pro-apoptotic/fibrotic gene expression, enhancing mitochondrial function, and maintaining ATP production [19,20]. Conversely, NMRK2 deletion activates p38 MAPK, impairs metabolic adaptation, and exacerbates cardiac dysfunction [21]. These data underscore the critical role of NMRK2 in preserving energy homeostasis and redox balance under stress conditions.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] NADPH acts as a critical electron donor for major antioxidant systems and is regenerated via NADK-mediated phosphorylation of NAD+ to NADP+ [[22], [23], [24]]. While NADK is indispensable for redox homeostasis, it has traditionally been viewed as a constitutive housekeeping enzyme with no described transcriptional control in the heart [[25], [26], [27]]. Given that NMRK2 is an integrin-binding protein known to interact with the YAP pathway [15,28], it is plausible that NMRK2 modulates NADK expression through YAP signaling. YAP is increasingly recognized for its critical roles in regulating cellular metabolism, oxidative stress responses, and myocardial regeneration and remodeling. Activation of YAP stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and enhances cardioprotective gene expression [29,30]

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Activation of YAP stimulates cardiomyocyte proliferation and enhances cardioprotective gene expression [29,30]. Additionally, epigenetic modifications of the Hippo-YAP pathway promote YAP translation, support myocardial regeneration, reduce infarct severity, and improve cardiac function [31,32]. However, the signaling cascades related to NMRK2 and NADK during myocardial I/R injury remain unclear.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] Here, we performed bioinformatic analysis of the GSE160516 dataset and identified NMRK2 as one of the most prominently upregulated genes within 24 h of reperfusion, a finding corroborated in our murine I/R model. Gain-of-function experiments showed that NMRK2 overexpression reduced infarct size, preserved myocardial architecture, and attenuated oxidative damage during myocardial I/R injury. NMRK2 overexpression also lowered cleaved-caspase 3 and cleaved-PARP while increasing SOD1, SOD2, Trx1 and Prdx1 expression. In cardiomyocytes subjected to H/R, NMRK2 improved cell viability, decreased apoptosis, and curtailed ROS generation. Quantitative metabolite analysis showed that NMRK2 restored NAD+/NADH and NADPH/NADP+ ratios, elevated GSH/GSSG, and enhanced Trx1 activity

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Quantitative metabolite analysis showed that NMRK2 restored NAD+/NADH and NADPH/NADP+ ratios, elevated GSH/GSSG, and enhanced Trx1 activity. These protective effects are completely abolished by NADK knockdown, establishing that NMRK2-mediated antioxidant defense is NADK-dependent.

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] Previous studies have reported the cardioprotective role of NMRK2 in ischemic cardiac injury and other cardiac diseases [9,10,18,21], but they primarily focused on the metabolic functions of NMRK2. Our work, however, reveals its dual role as both a metabolic and redox regulator. Our data provide the first evidence that NMRK2 rapidly upregulates NADK at the transcriptional level through a YAP-dependent mechanism., providing novel insight into NMRK2-mediated redox protection during myocardial I/R injury. As outlined in Fig. 14, NMRK2 acts as an early sensor of reperfusion stress and disrupts integrin β–YAP tethering at the cytosolic membrane, thereby releasing YAP for nuclear import. Inside the nucleus, YAP binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) and trans-activates NADK transcription

title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
text: [Discussion] . Inside the nucleus, YAP binds the NADK promoter (−1500 to −1000 bp) and trans-activates NADK transcription. Concomitantly, NMRK2-driven NAD+ salvage sustains NAD+/NADH balance and supplies substrate for the newly induced NADK. The resulting surge in NADP+/NADPH recharges the GSH and Trx systems, which in turn neutralize ROS and limit oxidative injury. Thus, by linking integrin-mediated mechanical signaling to YAP-dependent transcriptional control of NADPH regeneration, the NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis provides a coherent and translatable strategy for acute cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury.Fig. 14Schematic of NMRK2-mediated cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury

text: [Discussion] . 14Schematic of NMRK2-mediated cardioprotection against myocardial I/R injury. Under myocardial I/R conditions, NMRK2 reduces the integrin β–YAP interaction and facilitates YAP nuclear translocation. After entering the nucleus, YAP directly binds to the NADK promoter region (−1500 to −1000 bp) to promote NADK transcription. In parallel, NMRK2, as a key enzyme in NAD+ metabolism, contributes to maintain intracellular NAD+/NADH homeostasis and provide metabolic support for redox regulation. title: NMRK2–YAP–NADK axis preserves redox protection against myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] Chronic pain often involves abnormalities in central pain processing. Two commonly used experimental methods for central pain modulation are conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and offset analgesia (OA). However, it is uncertain how similar the underlying processes they measure are. Here, we applied CPM and OA in patients with fibromyalgia, a model disease of central sensitization, to explore these questions further.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] Fifty‐four female participants (27 fibromyalgia patients and 27 healthy participants) completed the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) and the McGill questionnaire and underwent CPM and OA in a randomised order.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] CPM and OA were positively correlated in healthy participants (R s = 0.40, p = 0.03) but negatively correlated in patients (R s = −0.47, p = 0.01). Additionally, we divided patients into responders and nonresponders for CPM and found that a significant negative correlation existed exclusively in nonresponders (R s = −0.64, p = 0.02), whereas no correlation existed in responders. Furthermore, CPM in patients was positively correlated with FIQ (R s = 0.4, p = 0.04) and McGill (R s = 0.65, p = 0.003), whereas OA was negatively correlated with both FIQ (R s = −0.445, p = 0.02) and McGill (R s = −0.47, p = 0.03).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] This study is the first to show that OA, not just CPM, is correlated with clinical features in fibromyalgia patients and that these two paradigms are inversely correlated and differentially related to disease symptomatology in fibromyalgia patients.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [abstract] This study is the first to demonstrate that conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and offset analgesia (OA) are inversely correlated in patients with fibromyalgia compared with healthy controls and show distinct associations with symptom severity. These findings reveal divergent mechanisms of central pain inhibition in chronic pain, highlighting the potential of both OA and CPM as novel markers for disease characterisation.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] Fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) is a chronic pain disorder characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain and systematic symptoms (Clauw 2009). Although a peripheral pain generator has not been conclusively identified, FMS has been associated with marked alterations in central nervous system (CNS) pain processing (Woolf 2011). These features have led to its classification under the emerging category of nociplastic pain—a mechanism‐based designation describing dysfunctional modulation of nociceptive signalling at multiple CNS levels rather than tissue injury—which is increasingly recognised as a core component of several primary centralised pain syndromes (Fitzcharles et al. 2021).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] Among the defining neurophysiological characteristics of nociplastic pain are reduced efficacy of endogenous pain inhibition and increased facilitation of nociceptive input (Arendt‐Nielsen 2015). Experimental paradigms such as conditioned pain modulation (CPM) and offset analgesia (OA) have been developed to probe these processes (Hermans et al. 2016).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] The CPM is a widely used proxy for descending inhibitory control, reflecting the capacity of a noxious conditioning stimulus to suppress the perception of a separate test stimulus (Nir and Yarnitsky 2015). This mechanism is believed to involve many brain areas, especially brainstem structures, particularly the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) (Nahman‐Averbuch and Timmers 2023). OA, by contrast, refers to a disproportionately large reduction in perceived pain following a minor decrease in stimulus intensity (Julien et al. 2005) and is thought to reflect cortically mediated temporal filtering, engaging regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and insula (Li et al. 2022).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] Unsurprisingly, impairments in both CPM and OA have been widely reported in FMS, which is consistent with dysregulated central pain modulation (Potvin and Marchand 2016; Oudejans et al. 2015). However, most studies have investigated these mechanisms in isolation, and only a few have assessed them concurrently in the same cohort (Honigman et al. 2013; Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014). Although CPM and OA are generally believed to rely on distinct mechanisms, each reflecting different aspects of endogenous pain modulation, the exact nature of the relationship between these two paradigms remains unclear and incompletely understood

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] . While both CPM and OA responses are typically preserved in healthy individuals, who usually demonstrate robust pain inhibitory capacity, there is nonetheless substantial interindividual variability in how effectively pain is modulated, even within healthy populations (Nuwailati et al. 2022). Importantly, from a clinical standpoint, it is still uncertain what it means to exhibit an intact CPM response in relation to OA and vice versa in healthy individuals; that is, whether individuals who show effective descending pain inhibition through CPM also demonstrate efficient temporal filtering of nociceptive input, as captured by OA

text: [Introduction] . Despite the limited body of research directly examining this relationship, only a few studies in healthy individuals have explored the relationships between these two paradigms within the same cohort, yielding significant (Honigman et al. 2013) and nonsignificant (Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014) results. This lack of consistency might be explained by the fact that although these tests probably manipulate distinct mechanisms, as discussed above, there is still considerable neural overlap in the brain areas that modulate them (Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014; Nahman‐Averbuch and Timmers 2023). Conversely, individuals with central chronic pain conditions, including FMS, demonstrate marked deficits in endogenous pain modulation, including in CPM and OA (Lewis et al. 2012)

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Introduction] The aim of this study was to examine the relationship between CPM and OA in individuals with FMS and in healthy controls, as both paradigms are widely used experimental measures of endogenous pain modulation. We tested two primary hypotheses. First, we hypothesized that the association between CPM and OA would differ between healthy individuals and patients with FMS, reflecting altered integration of pain modulatory mechanisms in FMS. Second, we hypothesized that CPM and OA abnormalities in FMS would be differentially related to clinical and disease‐specific symptoms, with each paradigm showing distinct associations with specific aspects of the FMS symptom profile

text: [Conditioned Pain Modulation] CPM was conducted via a parallel paradigm in which two identical noxious ‘test stimuli’ were applied: one before and one simultaneously with a noxious ‘conditioning stimulus’ (Granot et al. 2006; Nir and Yarnitsky 2015; Yarnitsky et al. 2015). Although sequential designs are often recommended to minimise attentional influences, previous studies (Pud et al. 2005; Yarnitsky et al. 2015) suggest that parallel CPM paradigms can produce stronger and more robust inhibitory effects than sequential paradigms can produce, possibly due to the overlapping activation of pain modulation circuits. This is particularly relevant in FMS, where descending inhibition is often impaired (Julien et al

text: [Conditioned Pain Modulation] . This is particularly relevant in FMS, where descending inhibition is often impaired (Julien et al. 2005) and where dynamic, concurrent stimulation may better reveal individual differences in pain modulation capacity. Additionally, the parallel design has been validated in multiple CPM studies involving both healthy individuals and patients with chronic pain, including FMS (Yarnitsky et al. 2008). This makes it a widely accepted and standardised protocol for comparative studies in clinical populations.

Following a 15‐min break, the nondominant hand was immersed in a cold‐water bath (up to the wrist) for 60 s

text: [Conditioned Pain Modulation] . Following a 15‐min break, the nondominant hand was immersed in a cold‐water bath (up to the wrist) for 60 s. During the final 30 s of immersion, the ‘test stimulus’ was reapplied, and the participants rated their pain intensity again at three time points (0, 15 and 30 s after the reapplication of the test stimulus). The CPM magnitude was determined by subtracting the average pain ratings obtained from the test stimulus alone (Ts_alone) from the average rating obtained when the test stimulus was applied simultaneously with the conditioned stimulus (Ts_conditioned). Negative values indicate inhibitory (effective) CPM.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Offset Analgesia] The OA was implemented via a three‐temperature paradigm for the volar aspect of the dominant arm (Ligato et al. 2018; Szikszay et al. 2019). The temperature of the heat probe was increased at a rate of 2°C per second from a baseline of 32°C to the individual's test temperature (VAS60 temperature), which was held constant for 5 s. The temperature was then raised to 1°C for another 5 s before the samples were returned to the individual's test temperature (a decrease of 1°C). This temperature was maintained for 20 s, followed by a rapid return to the baseline temperature at a rate of 5°C per second. We defined the initial temperature increase reaching VAS 60 as T1, the 1°C increase maintained for 5 s as T2 and the phase of returning to the VAS 60 temperature, held for 20 s, as T3.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Offset Analgesia] The participants sequentially rated the intensity of the perceived pain via a computerised visual analog scale (CoVAS) device. The magnitude of OA was computed by subtracting the peak CoVAS score at T2 from the minimum CoVAS score within the initial 10 s of T3 (Kobinata et al. 2017). A negative OA magnitude indicates efficient OA.

text: [Offset Analgesia] OA was conducted over three trials, with each trial separated by an interstimulus interval of at least 5 min. The thermode was slightly moved to reduce habituation between trials. The final OA magnitude was calculated by averaging the results from all three trials, with outliers excluded. Outliers were identified via Z scores, and values greater than 3 or less than −3 were excluded from the analysis (Ligato et al. 2018; Oudejans et al. 2015; Szikszay et al. 2021).

text: [Discussion] This study directly examined, for the first time, the relationship between two widely used experimental paradigms probing central pain modulation, CPM and OA, in healthy participants and in patients with chronic pain, specifically FMS, which is often conceptualised as a test case of a central sensitization syndrome. As expected, FMS patients presented substantially lower levels of both CPM and OA than healthy participants. In addition, our results indicate that these two indices of supraspinal pain modulation are inversely related in patients with FMS, in contrast to the pattern observed in healthy controls

text: [Discussion] . Furthermore, the paradigms exhibit divergent relationships with clinical symptomatology, such that greater disease severity is associated with deficient (non‐inhibitory) CPM but, conversely, with enhanced OA.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] Studies investigating endogenous pain modulation in chronic pain patients have revealed diminished pain‐related activity within inhibitory pathways, explicitly involving the rostral anterior cingulate cortex (rACC), the PAG and the RVM (Harper et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2018). Both CPM and OA serve as experimental measures used to assess endogenous pain modulation, but they are not identical. In addition to their different psychophysical properties, where CPM relies on a secondary painful stimulus (Nir and Yarnitsky 2015) and OA responds to changes in the intensity of a single painful stimulus (Ligato et al. 2018), a variance in the central mechanisms involved in each paradigm has been suggested (Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014).

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] CPM refers to the reduction in perceived pain of an ongoing painful stimulus following the application of a separate conditioning noxious stimulus. This process heavily involves descending inhibitory pathways originating in the PAG and RVM, which release endogenous opioids and serotonin to dampen spinal‐level pain signalling (Sprenger et al. 2011). Although CPM engages higher‐order regions such as the ACC and PFC, its primary mechanism for inhibiting pain relies predominantly on brainstem‐driven descending modulation. Cortical areas contribute by providing some attentional and emotional modulation (Nahman‐Averbuch and Timmers 2023). However, these cortical influences are less critical to the main inhibitory effect of CPM (Ossipov et al. 2010)

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] . However, these cortical influences are less critical to the main inhibitory effect of CPM (Ossipov et al. 2010). Accordingly, CPM provides more sustained modulation in the presence of the conditioning stimulus. This gradual effect persists with the secondary stimulus, reflecting the slower, steady nature of descending inhibition.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] OA, in contrast, is triggered by a minor decrease in the intensity of a single painful stimulus, leading to a disproportionately large reduction in perceived pain. Although this response engages brainstem regions such as the PAG and RVM, it is particularly sensitive to dynamic changes in pain intensity. This process relies more strongly on cortical regions, including the ACC, PFC and insula, which rapidly detect subtle stimulus changes and recalibrate pain perception through a combination of top‐down and sensory mechanisms (Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014; Yelle et al. 2008). Thus, OA produces a rapid and short‐lived analgesic effect that occurs almost immediately after a reduction in stimulus intensity

text: [Discussion] Various pharmacological studies have indicated differences between the two paradigms. For example, in patients with diabetic polyneuropathy, opioid agonists increase CPM effectiveness (Niesters et al. 2014). In contrast, neither opioid agonists nor antagonists had any effect on OA in individuals experiencing opioid‐induced hyperalgesia (Martucci et al. 2012). Furthermore, administering an SNRI enhances CPM in patients with diabetic neuropathies (Yarnitsky et al. 2012), whereas a drug from the same class does not affect OA in healthy individuals (Olesen et al. 2018)

Moreover, a recent study from our group revealed that the psychoactive cannabinoid component Δ9‐tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) exerts differential effects on these two pain modulation paradigms in FMS, as it enhanced OA but did not significantly alter CPM, further supporting the interpretation that OA and CPM could rely on partially distinct underlying mechanisms (Agbaria et al. 2025). These variations may help to further clarify the distinctions between the paradigms, although the research remains inconclusive (France et al. 2016; Okkerse et al. 2017).

text: [Discussion] Importantly, the short‐term discontinuation of centrally acting medications before testing may have influenced CPM and OA in this study. On one hand, medication withdrawal may have reduced any direct pharmacological enhancement or suppression of descending pain modulation. On the other hand, early discontinuation or rebound effects may have transiently altered pain sensitivity, arousal, mood and sleep‐related factors. These changes could, in turn, affect psychophysical pain paradigms and increase between‐subject variability.

title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] This issue is particularly relevant for SNRIs, as discontinuation symptoms can emerge within days of cessation. Accordingly, a 48‐h washout may not fully eliminate pharmacologic exposure for all compounds and may, in some individuals, bias CPM and OA estimates toward reduced apparent inhibitory capacity and/or greater variability. However, because only six FMS patients discontinued such medications (four of whom used SNRIs), any impact on group‐level conclusions is likely limited. Future studies should consider longer, compound‐specific washout periods or fully medication‐free cohorts when feasible.

text: [Discussion] We observed a significant positive association between CPM and OA in the healthy cohort, indicating that participants who exhibited stronger CPM inhibition also tended to show a greater OA effect (i.e., greater pain reduction following offset). This pattern is consistent with the notion that while CPM and OA reflect partially distinct dimensions of endogenous modulation (spatial vs. temporal filtering), they may still share overlapping inhibitory components at the individual‐differences level (Honigman et al. 2013; Nahman‐Averbuch et al. 2014).

However, these findings differ from those of Nahman‐Averbuch et al. Even when CPM appears ‘preserved’, FMS responders may still differ from controls in other state and trait level factors (ongoing pain, hypervigilance, fatigue and affective or cognitive load) that can disrupt the coupling between spatial (CPM) and temporal (OA) inhibitory processes. One explanation is a ‘range restriction’ effect: by definition, CPM responders cluster toward inhibitory values, which can reduce between‐subject variability and attenuate correlations with OA, particularly in modest sample sizes

text: [Discussion] Consistent with this, studies directly assessing both paradigms in the same individuals report that OA and CPM are not necessarily tightly coupled, supporting the interpretation that preserved OA with impaired CPM (or vice versa) can occur depending on which neural or cognitive processes are most affected (Agbaria et al. 2025; Hermans et al. 2016; Vollert et al. 2022). In FMS, this divergence is biologically plausible. Impairments in CPM are commonly interpreted as reflecting reduced efficacy of descending inhibitory control, representing an altered balance between inhibition and facilitation. In contrast, OA may be more sensitive to perceptual gain or contrast mechanisms, which can be amplified in states of central sensitization or hypervigilance

text: [Discussion] Taken together, our findings, along with broader evidence demonstrating that OA and CPM can be differentially modulated across chronic pain conditions and experimental contexts, support the view that OA and CPM provide complementary information about pain modulation. These paradigms may therefore aid in stratifying patients into subgroups with distinct dominant alterations. For example, some patients may show impaired spatial inhibitory control, whereas others may exhibit altered temporal contrast processing. This approach is consistent with the increasing emphasis on mechanism‐informed patient stratification, rather than presuming a uniform deficit in descending inhibitory function across all chronic pain populations (Hermans et al. 2016).

text: [Discussion] In the present study, we detected abnormalities in the CPM response in FMS patients that positively correlated with abnormalities in FIQ and McGill scores. However, we also present novel evidence for a correlation between these disease‐specific scores and OA in FMS. Accordingly, OA may similarly be used to estimate disease load and possibly to categorise patients into endophenotypes that may characterise pathophysiologic profiles or predict response and prognosis. Further studies are needed to examine the applicability and validity of using OA for these aims.

This finding may indicate that the relative contributions of OA and CPM to overall pain modulation vary depending on the degree of descending inhibition. title: Differential Alterations in Offset Analgesia and Conditioned Pain Modulation in Fibromyalgia: Evidence for Distinct Central Dysregulation
text: [Discussion] The findings of this study underscore the potential clinical significance of CPM and OA measures in chronic pain patients, as their divergent patterns in FMS may help identify subgroups of patients with different modulatory profiles. Such distinctions could be clinically valuable for patient phenotyping and classification and may guide the development of personalised treatment strategies targeting specific deficits in central pain modulation. For example, patients with impaired CPM but preserved OA may benefit from therapies aimed at restoring tonic descending inhibition (e.g., certain antidepressants or exercise‐based interventions), whereas others may require broader neuromodulatory approaches.

text: [Discussion] Future studies should integrate both OA and CPM within the same experimental framework to investigate whether individual differences in these pain modulation processes predict treatment response over time. These findings may provide deeper insights into the distinct roles of CPM and OA in FMS and other chronic pain conditions. Moreover, future studies involving pharmacological manipulations of both CPM and OA could be highly valuable for advancing our understanding of the mechanisms underlying these paradigms.

text: [Limitations] This study has limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the presence of peripheral neuropathic pain was not objectively verified in this study and was instead based on participant self‐reports, which may be incomplete or inaccurate and could have introduced misclassification and additional variability in the psychophysical test outcomes. Furthermore, pain and FMS‐specific questionnaires were administered only to the FMS group; although controls were screened to be free of chronic pain, collecting a harmonised questionnaire set in controls would have enabled more direct group comparability and clearer interpretation of potential floor effects

text: [Limitations] . Another limitation is missing data for some questionnaires, which could have reduced the effective sample size for questionnaire‐based analyses. A further limitation is that CPM was assessed via a parallel design (test stimulus delivered during conditioning). CPM practice recommendations note that simultaneous presentation may recruit attentional/cognitive modulation, potentially limiting interpretation as purely descending inhibition. Finally, the relatively small sample size (N = 27 per group) also restricts the statistical power and may limit the generalizability of the findings to larger or more diverse populations.
